quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009s-01.prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite group of order $p(p + 1)$, where $p$ is an odd prime, and assume that $G$ does not have a normal Sylow $p$-subgroup.

(a) Find (with proof) the number of elements of $G$ with order different from $p$.

(b) Show that each nonidentity conjugacy class of elements with order different from $p$ has size at least $p$, and conclude that there is precisely one such conjugacy class.

(c) Prove that $p + 1$ is a power of $2$.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009s-01.answer:
(a) $n_p=p+1$, the Sylow $p$-subgroups have order $p$ and meet trivially, so there are $p^2-1$ elements of order $p$ and $p+1$ elements of order $
e p$. (b) $N_G(P)=P$, so no element of order $p$ centralizes an $x
e1$ of order $
e p$; thus $p$ divides each such class size, and the $p$ such elements form a single class. (c) All nonidentity elements of order $
eq p$ are conjugate, so have the same order; for each prime $q\mid p+1$ that order is a power of $q$, so $p+1$ has one prime divisor, namely $2$.

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009s-02.prompt:
Let $\mathbb R$ be the field of real numbers and let $\mathbb C\supseteq\mathbb R$ be the complex field. Define $S$ to be the subring of the polynomial ring $\mathbb C[X]$ consisting of all polynomials with real constant term so that
$$S = \mathbb R + \mathbb CX + \mathbb CX^2 + \mathbb CX^3 + \cdots.$$

(a) Show that the ideal of $S$ consisting of all polynomials with $0$ constant term is not principal.

(b) Let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of $S$ and choose $0\ne f\in I$ to have minimal possible degree $n$. If $g\in I$, show that there exists $s\in S$ with $g - sf$ either equal to $0$ or to a polynomial of degree $n$. Conclude that $I$ is generated by $f$ and perhaps one additional polynomial of degree $n$.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009s-02.answer: (a) A generator would be $cX$, but the $X$-coefficients of $cX\cdot S$ form the real line $c\mathbb R$, which cannot contain both $1$ and $i$. (b) Kill leading terms with $s=(g_m/f_n)X^{m-n}\in S$ while $\deg g>n$; the elements of $I$ of degree $\le n$ form a real vector space injecting into $\mathbb C$ via the $X^n$-coefficient, so they are spanned over $\mathbb R$ by $f$ and at most one more $h$, and $I=fS+hS$.

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009s-03.prompt:
Let $F$ be the field $GF(p)$ of prime order $p > 2$ and suppose that the polynomial $f(X) = X^m + 1\in F[X]$ is irreducible.

(a) Show that every root of $f$ in a splitting field of the polynomial has multiplicative order $2m$.

(b) Prove that $2m$ divides $p^m - 1$, but that $2m$ does not divide $p^n - 1$ for any integer $n$ with $0 < n < m$.

(c) Show that $m \ne 4$.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009s-03.answer: (a) $\theta^{2m}=1\ne\theta^m$; if the order were $d<2m$ then $d$ is even and $\theta^{d/2}=-1$, making $\theta$ a root of $X^{d/2}+1$ of degree $<m$. (b) $\theta$ generates $GF(p^m)^\times\supseteq\langle\theta\rangle$; if $2m\mid p^n-1$ then $\theta\in GF(p^n)$, so $m\le n$. (c) $p^2\equiv1\pmod 8$ for odd $p$, so $8\mid p^2-1$, contradicting (b) for $m=4$.

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009s-04.prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over the complex numbers $\mathbb C$ and let $T\colon V\to V$ be a linear operator on $V$.

(a) If $T$ is diagonalizable on $V$ and if $W$ is a subspace of $V$ with $T(W)\subseteq W$, prove that $T$ is diagonalizable on $W$.

(b) If $T$ has the matrix
$$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ 2 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$$
with respect to some basis of $V$, decide (with proof) whether $T$ is diagonalizable on $V$.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009s-04.answer: (a) The minimal polynomial of $T|_W$ divides that of $T$, a product of distinct linear factors. (b) Not diagonalizable: the characteristic polynomial is $x^2(x-1)$ but the matrix has rank $2$, so the $0$-eigenspace is only $1$-dimensional (equivalently $A(A-I)\ne0$).

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009s-05.prompt:
In the following, all groups are additive abelian groups, and recall that an abelian group is said to be noetherian if its set of subgroups satisfies the ascending chain condition or equivalently the maximal condition. Furthermore, a nonzero group is said to be uniform if it contains no direct sum of nonzero subgroups.

(a) Show that every nonzero noetherian group contains a nonzero uniform subgroup.

(b) Suppose $G = U \dotplus V$ is the internal direct sum of the two subgroups $U$ and $V$ with $U$ uniform. If $G$ contains the direct sum $A \dotplus B$ with $A$ and $B$ both nonzero, prove that $(A\dotplus B)\cap V \ne 0$.

(c) Let $G = U\dotplus V$ be as above with $U$ uniform. If $G$ contains the direct sum $A\dotplus B\dotplus C$ with $A$, $B$ and $C$ all nonzero, prove that $V$ is not uniform.
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2009s-05.answer: (a) Otherwise split off nonzero summands forever, $A_1\subsetneq A_1\dotplus A_2\subsetneq\cdots$, violating ACC. (b) If $(A\dotplus B)\cap V=0$, the projection onto $U$ is injective on $A\dotplus B$ and gives a direct sum of two nonzero subgroups in $U$. (c) If $V$ were uniform, the nonzero groups $X=(A\dotplus B)\cap V$, $Y=(A\dotplus C)\cap V$, $Z=(B\dotplus C)\cap V$ would pairwise meet, giving $A\cap V\ne0\ne B\cap V$, two nonzero subgroups of $V$ with zero intersection.
